query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In lightweight high‐entropy alloys, the deliberate incorporation of passivating elements (such as Cr and Al) enables the in situ formation of a continuous, coherent oxide scale (e.g., a merged Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer) under high-temperature conditions, which simultaneously hinders oxygen diffusion (thereby improving oxidation and corrosion resistance) and stabilizes the microstructure (thus preserving mechanical strength). In contrast, alloys lacking these elements develop non‐uniform and spalling oxide films that degrade both environmental stability and mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight high‐entropy alloy composed of a multi–element solid solution system without specific enhancement for passivation.
generation.intervention: Introduce passivating alloying elements (for example, Cr and Al) into the alloy composition to promote protective oxide layer formation.
generation.conditions: Expose both the passivated and non–passivated baseline alloys to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 900 °C) in air and corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5% NaCl solution) under identical processing and service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, dense oxide scale (principally an integrated Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer) that impedes oxygen ingress and stabilizes the internal microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The added passivating elements oxidize preferentially to form a coherent oxide film, which functions as a barrier to further oxygen transport, reduces internal oxidation, and helps maintain a refined and stable microstructure that underpins mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy with Cr and Al will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate (evidenced by reduced weight gain and higher oxide film density), enhanced corrosion resistance (demonstrated by lower corrosion current densities and higher pitting potentials) and minimal degradation in mechanical performance under high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: An otherwise similar lightweight high–entropy alloy that lacks targeted passivating elements, resulting in a less uniform, spalling oxide scale and diminished environmental and mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may cease to hold if the operating temperatures are high enough to induce excessive grain growth or if the diffusional kinetics lead to excessive interdiffusion that prevents the maintenance of a continuous passivating layer, or if non–passivating secondary phases form and dominate the microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: While existing observations on similar alloys suggest that passivating elements improve oxidation and corrosion resistance, the precise quantitative contributions to mechanical retention and the interplay with microstructural evolution in lightweight high–entropy alloys remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of lightweight high–entropy alloy samples with identical base matrices: one set with the addition of high proportions of passivating elements (e.g., Cr and Al) and a control set without these elements. Process both sets under identical manufacturing conditions. Expose the samples to isothermal oxidation at 900 °C in air and perform corrosion tests in 3.5% NaCl solution. Additionally, evaluate mechanical properties before and after exposure.
measurements: Weight gain during high–temperature oxidation (to assess oxidation rate)
Cross–sectional microscopy and XRD analysis of the oxide scales (to evaluate oxide scale continuity and composition)
Electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS) for corrosion resistance
Mechanical testing (compression/tensile strength) pre– and post–exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated alloy (with Cr and Al) does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance (i.e., reduced weight gain and denser oxide scales), enhanced corrosion metrics (lower corrosion current density and higher pitting potential), and better retention of mechanical properties compared to the control alloy, then the hypothesis that the passivating elements mediate these combined benefits is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To explore the types of oxides, XRD analysis was performed on the surface of the coatings after oxidation. As shown in Figure 9, the oxide mainly consists of CrTaO4, TiO2, and Cr2O3; the Cr1 alloy has the highest oxide diffraction peak, indicating that more oxides are generated, making the oxide film on the coating surface uniform and dense. The dense oxide film inhibits the diffusion of oxygen atoms, reduces the oxidation rate, and improves oxidation resistance. This conclusion is also consistent with the results presented by the oxide weight-gain curve. The results show that adding Cr to the WVTaTi alloy can effectively improve high-temperature oxidation resistance.

cited_evidence.text: As observed during the isothermal oxidation process, the outer oxide layers of the FeNiCuAlCo and FeNiCuAlMn HEAs develop wrinkles, while the inner oxide layers bend and may even detach from the substrate (Figure 7b,c), leading to the formation of an irregular oxide layer. In contrast, the oxide film of the FeNiCuAlCr HEA is denser and remains free of cracks. Figure 8 is a schematic of the oxidation mechanism of FeNiCuAlCr alloys in air at 900 °C. In the oxidation process of FeNiCuAlCr high-entropy alloys, Al2O3 initially forms on the surface, where it acts as a passivating layer, preventing further oxygen diffusion and thereby limiting the oxidation of internal elements. Subsequently, chromium oxide and copper oxide layers form. As the oxidation progresses, the Al2O3 and Cr2O3 oxide layers grow thicker and merge, with oxygen gradually migrating inward. Over time, under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the system reaches local equilibrium in oxygen partial pressure, leading to the formation of continuous spinel-type oxides (NiFe2O4) due to reactions between Ni and Fe oxides. These factors contribute to the excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance of FeNiCuAlCr alloys.

In this study, the oxidation behavior of the FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated in air at 900 °C, and their corrosion resistance in 3.5% NaCl solution was evaluated using potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The following conclusions were drawn:(1)The oxidation kinetics of the FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn HEAs in air at 900 °C follow a parabolic relationship. Among them, the FeNiCuAlCr HEA exhibited excellent oxidation resistance, with a low mass gain of 0.83 mg/cm2 after 108 h of exposure at 900 °C.(2)The outer oxidation layer of the FeNiCuAlCr HEA formed a dense and continuous Al2O3 and Cr2O3 layer, which provided effective protection for the substrate. In contrast, for the FeNiCuAlCo and FeNiCuAlMn HEAs, prolonged oxidation and increased high-temperature internal stress led to the partial peeling and wrinkling of the oxide scale at the interface between the scale and the alloy.(3)The electrochemical analysis revealed that the FeNiCuAlCr HEA possesses a high corrosion potential (Ecorr = −0.21 V) and a low corrosion current density (Icorr = 45.7 μA/cm2).
